overview.intro: Section A carries 26 of the 80 theory marks, and 18 of those come from two unseen passages answered by multiple choice questions. The paper is not testing whether you know the subject of the passage — it is testing whether you can locate, interpret and evaluate what a text actually says under time pressure. This unit works through the method: how to read for structure before detail, how the two passage types differ, how to answer inference and vocabulary items honestly, and how the case-based passage with charts and data is meant to be read.

learningOutcomes: Identify the structure and claim of an unseen passage before reading for detail.

learn.title: A method that works on any passage

blocks.text: Read the passage once for structure, not for facts. Note in the margin what each paragraph does — sets the scene, states a claim, gives evidence, qualifies, concludes — because most inference questions are really questions about what a paragraph is doing. Then read the questions, and take each one back to the paragraph it belongs to rather than trusting a phrase you half-remember. The examiner’s wrong options are built from real words in the passage: an option that repeats four words from paragraph two and contradicts its fifth is designed to look right, so the test is whether you check the relationship between the words and not merely their presence.

learn.title: Reading the first passage: factual, descriptive or literary

blocks.text: The first passage is straight comprehension with a vocabulary component, drawn from factual, descriptive or literary writing. Factual passages argue or inform, so the load-bearing sentence is usually the topic sentence, often first or last in a paragraph, with the rest supplying example or qualification. Descriptive passages move through scenes or aspects of a subject, so the risk is losing the thread of sequence; a quick note of what each paragraph describes keeps you oriented. Literary passages — a narrative excerpt or reflective essay — carry meaning in tone and image, so inference questions there depend on how something is said rather than only on what is said.

Vocabulary items in this passage ask for the meaning of a word as used in the sentence. The reliable technique is substitution: put each option into the sentence in place of the original word and read it aloud in your head. If the sentence stops making sense, the option is out. Watch for words with several common meanings — light, reserved, checked, qualified — where the passage’s context selects a sense the first option on the list does not have.

items.text: A sentence reading “the results were qualified by later evidence”.
items.note: Qualified means limited or hedged, not certified — the later evidence narrowed the claim.

items.text: An option that repeats three words from the passage but reverses a relation.
items.note: Word-matching is the commonest trap: check who did what to whom.

learn.title: Reading the second passage: case-based with data and visuals

blocks.text: The second passage is case-based and includes verbal or visual inputs such as tables, charts and statistical data. It is marked for evaluation, which means some questions ask what the evidence supports rather than what the text says. Before reading the body, read the visual: what is on each axis, what unit is used, over what period, and what the source is. A chart of percentages and a chart of absolute numbers can both rise while telling opposite stories about the same case, and an option that swaps one for the other is a standard distractor.

Treat the case and the visuals as one document. Where a question refers to a figure, verify the number against the visual rather than against your memory of the paragraph, and beware options that invert a comparison — “twice as high” against “half as high” is the same pair of numbers read in opposite directions. Where the passage draws a conclusion, check whether the data in the visual actually warrants it: an association over a short period is not proof of cause, and an option that claims causation from correlation is usually the wrong one.

rows: Percentages and totals behave differently in comparison
A short window can reverse a long trend

blocks.text: The marks available here are large and cheap compared with the writing section: 18 marks for reading plus 8 for the notes that follow. A workable allocation within Section A is to read each passage once carefully, answer as you go, and revisit only the items you flagged. The commonest losses are not failures of comprehension but of discipline: choosing an option because it shares words with the passage, importing outside knowledge that the passage does not contain, and misreading a chart axis under time pressure.

Practice should therefore be done under a timer with review, not at leisure. After each attempt, classify every error: located the wrong paragraph, read the sentence correctly but generalised, misread the visual, or ran out of time. The classification matters because each cause has a different correction — re-reading, restraint, axis-checking or pacing. Students who review by cause rather than by score are the ones whose accuracy rises week by week.

questions.prompt: The combined word limit for the two unseen passages in the CBSE Class XI paper is:
questions.explanation: The curriculum fixes the combined word limit for both passages at 600–750 words.

questions.prompt: The second passage in Section A differs from the first mainly because it:
options: Is case-based and carries verbal or visual inputs such as data and charts
Is taken from the prescribed literature
questions.answer: Is case-based and carries verbal or visual inputs such as data and charts
questions.explanation: The case-based passage adds statistical and visual inputs and is marked for evaluation rather than recall alone.

questions.prompt: A passage states that sales rose for three months while profits fell. The option “higher sales caused higher profits” is wrong because:
options: The passage says nothing about profits
The two trends moved in opposite directions in the period given
Profit is not mentioned in the chart
questions.answer: The two trends moved in opposite directions in the period given
questions.explanation: The data given shows the two moving in opposite directions, so the option contradicts the evidence rather than summarising it.

questions.prompt: The word “reserved” in the sentence “her reserved manner fooled nobody” most nearly means:
questions.explanation: Substitution in context rules out the other senses of the word: only “restrained and quiet” fits the sentence.

questions.prompt: Before reading the values in a chart, a reader should check its axis, unit, period and __________ .
questions.explanation: The source and sample tell you what population the figures describe and how far they generalise.

questions.prompt: A wrong option that repeats words from the passage while reversing who did what to whom is called a __________ .
questions.explanation: Distractors are built from the passage’s own vocabulary, which is why word-matching alone fails.

questions.prompt: State four steps of a reliable method for answering questions on an unseen passage.
questions.answer: Four steps are: skim the passage once for structure and note what each paragraph does; read the questions before hunting for details; return each question to the paragraph it belongs to and mark the sentence that holds the evidence; and test every option against that sentence rather than accepting the one that shares words with the passage. Reserving a fixed time block for the passage set is also accepted.
questions.explanation: Each step must be an action the reader takes, not a general exhortation to read carefully.

questions.prompt: How does answering a case-based passage differ from answering a factual one?
questions.answer: A factual passage is answered by locating what the text states and inferring only what it supports, so the skill is precision of location and restraint in generalising. A case-based passage adds verbal or visual inputs — tables, charts, statistical data — and its questions are marked for evaluation, so the reader must first read the visual itself: what the axes show, the unit used, the period covered and the source. The answer must then be checked against the figure rather than against memory of the prose, and claims of cause must be tested against what the data actually establishes, since an association over a short period does not prove causation. In short, the factual passage rewards careful reading while the case-based passage rewards careful measurement as well.
questions.explanation: Both methods must be described with the additional checks the visual input requires.

questions.prompt: Explain how inference questions are built, and describe how to answer them without being trapped.
questions.answer: Inference questions ask for what a text implies rather than what it states, and they are the item type most often answered wrongly because the wrong option is usually believable rather than absurd. Exam builders construct these options in three ways. The first is over-generalisation: the passage supports a claim about one group, season or instance, and the option quietly extends it to all groups or times, so “some readers found the argument persuasive” becomes “readers found the argument persuasive”. The second is relation inversion: every noun in the option appears in the passage, but the direction of cause, blame or sequence is reversed, so word-matching confirms an option that meaning contradicts. The third is outside knowledge: the option is true in the world but absent from the passage, which is irrelevant in a comprehension item. The method that defeats all three is the same. Take the option back to the paragraph, find the single sentence that would confirm or refute it, and require that sentence to support the whole of the option including its qualifiers — its scope, its degree and its causal direction. If the evidence supports only part of the option, the option is wrong, because an inference must follow from the text rather than sit alongside it. Practice makes this fast: the student who reviews missed items by asking “which word in my option did the passage not authorise?” stops losing marks to plausibility.
questions.explanation: Full marks need the three constructions of distractors and the sentence-level test applied to each.

questions.prompt: “Marks in this section are lost to carelessness rather than to lack of comprehension.” Discuss with reference to how the questions are designed.
questions.answer: There is substantial truth in the claim, because the paper is designed to reward precision. The questions are objective, which means every wrong answer comes from choosing rather than from an inability to write; the passages are within ordinary reading ability; and the distractors are built from the passage’s own words, so a reader who comprehends but does not verify will select them. Misreading a chart axis, missing a negative, or generalising a claim the text limited to one case — each of these costs a mark that comprehension alone would have earned. The case-based passage with statistical inputs makes the point sharply: two options describing the same figures in opposite directions both look familiar, and only checking the axis separates them. The counter-argument is that some items genuinely test reading ability rather than care. Vocabulary in context requires a reader to hold several senses of a word and select by context; inference across paragraphs requires holding a line of reasoning rather than a phrase; and evaluation of whether data warrants a conclusion is a higher-order skill that carelessness cannot supply at all. For these items a careless reader and an incapable reader converge on the same wrong answer for different reasons. The balanced judgement is that the section is weighted toward items where discipline pays immediately — location, verification, restraint — while retaining a minority whose difficulty lies in interpretation itself. Practically, the claim is useful as a training diagnosis: most recoverable marks here come from verification habits, which is why error review by cause raises scores faster than additional undirected reading.
questions.explanation: Full marks require evidence from the design of the item types, the counter-examples where skill dominates, and a judgement that separates the two populations of errors.
